text: Resistance: Friend or Foe? MITCHELL MAY, M,S,W., B,C,D,* This paper shows resistances in a benign light. The view is presented that psychoanalysts able to view resistances in a friendly light as challenges and guides, rather than as onerous roadblocks, experience maximum success for the patient and maximum satisfaction for themselves. The use of psychoanalytic technique to this end is demonstrated. INTRODUCTION When patients enter my consulting room to begin analysis, they are in pain but they don't understand why. They are not aware that the pain is the result of unconscious conflicts and compromise formations that can cause dis- abling symptoms: anxiety reactions, depressive affect, phobias, and compul- sive acts. We all have wishes, fantasies, and desires based on libidinal (sexual and aggressive) drive derivatives. These are constantly pressing for discharge and are cathected with a great amount of psychic energy. At the same time, a counter-cathexis of energy blocks off the ego's capacity to master the excitation and stimulation of these derivatives, "The neurotic conflict, by definition, is one between a tendency striving for discharge and another tendency that tries to prevent this discharge"' (p. 129), This conflict takes place between the id and the ego. The psychoanalytic theory of conflict has been expanded by Brenner^ who states, "It is unpleasure that is responsible for defense and conflict, in connection with infantile instinctual wishes and, further, that this unpleasure is of two kinds, anxiety and what I call depressive affect" (p. 7), It is the analyst who must understand patients in ways they cannot understand themselves by exploring with them a world new to them, the world of the unconscious. In order to unlock, enter, and journey through the unconscious, the analyst must be an authority of unconscious processes with an in-depth knowledge of psychoanalytic theory and technique. This knowl- edge when coupled with empathy enables the analyst to learn how patients relate (transference) who, then, can bring into consciousness the uncon- *Director, New York Center for Psychoanalytic Training. Mailing address: 320 West 90th Street, NewYork, NY 10024. AMEMCAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY, Vol, 50, No, 1, Winter 1996 32 Resistance: Friend or Foe? scious world of the patient. For patients to change and grow, their ego- syntonic behaviors and character traits must become ego-dystonic so they may experience them consciously and thereby expand the ego. When the unconscious becomes conscious, the ego expands and can tolerate the stimulation, excitation, frustration, and anxiety produced. At that point, patients use this conscious information to help change their lives. Psychoanaly- sis is an emotional experience, not an intellectual process. By making the unconscious conscious, patients can and do develop insights leading to change, growth and the attainment of love but the route is seldom direct since patients are not aware of resistances. Resistance is a defense against insight. There is always a reason, often multiple reasons, why patients use a specific resistance. Both the analyst and patients must be comfortable with the search for them. Patients can never be comfortable with the search if the analyst is not. The more pejorative the analyst is toward resistances, the more resistant patients will hecome. The analyst must help patients become friendly with the resistances thereby turning the work into an exploration rather than a battle. Even the word "resistance" can be anxiety producing. In the beginning of an analysis, it is useful to help patients become aware that they are not aware. To work with the anxiety produced by not knowing at the beginning of treatment launches the patients' role of exploration into the unknown. Careful attention must be paid by the analyst to any anxiety produced in patients at the point they begin to become aware that they are not aware of unconscious motivations. By sensitively, consistently and empathetically, exploring with patients the discomfort about not knowing, the course of analysis becomes an explora- tion. I tell patients, "The answers are inside of you. I will explore with you what they are." To speak of "exploring the unknown" with patients is, then, less likely to create fear in both patient and analyst than to use the word "resistance." The same holds true in the process of teaching/supervising where candidates/supervisees need to approach the work as exploration without accusations of resisting the material. Resistance is not an enemy; it is simply part of the exploration ahead for both the analyst and patients. It is a major part of our work and we, the analysts, need to make friends with the resistances ourselves. Resistances are our guides, not our enemies. Resis- tances are an essential part of every individual's character structure. They may, and do at times, impede the course of an analysis. As stated by many authors, all analyses must be carried on in the face of some resistance. All through the writings of Freud, he consistently discusses resistance. In the Interpretation of Dreams,^ he writes about censorship due to resistance stating, "Whatever interrupts the progress of analytic work is a resistance" 33 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY (p. 517). In The Dynamics of Transference,'* he writes the transference is the most frequent cause of resistance (p. 101). In Psychoanalysis,' he states, "The analytic theory of the neurosis is based on three cornerstones: the recognition of (1) 'repression,' of (2) the importance of the sexual instinct and of (3) 'transference' "(p. 267 ). In the same paper Freud points out, "There is a force in the mind which exercises the functions of a censorship, and which excludes from consciousness and from any influence upon action all tendencies which displease it. Such tendencies are described as 're- pressed'. They remain unconscious; and if one attempts to bring them into the patient's consciousness, one provokes a 'resistance' " (p. 267). If we accept the idea of becoming friendly with resistance, resistances become less onerous and more benign in analysis, in teaching, and in supervising. Boredom and impatience with patients can be replaced by the adventure of understanding how resistances developed in a way that creates an exciting journey for analyst and analysand. Boredom gives over to excitement when the analyst concentrates on determining why patients need to repeat. The analyst who generates internal excitement helps patients develop the excitement and the willingness to search for those reasons. The analyst who gets bored and impatient with patients' repetitions has devel- oped a counterresistance toward the resistances of patients and the work at hand is impeded. Strean^ states "Resistance is considered to be a universal phenomenon in all therapy, and all clients, despite their suffering want to preserve the status quo. Similarly, counter-resistance is a universal phenom- enon and all therapists want to preserve their own status quo"(p. 2). In order to make the unconscious conscious, the repression must be lifted. Often, many different forms of resistances are at work through which one must travel before reaching the repressed memory, the affect, the idea that initially caused the trauma and psychic pain that had to be repressed. This can be arduous work unless we can look upon it as an exciting, stimulating, and libidinally satisfying challenge for both analyst and analy- sand. The value, not only of helping patients become friendly with these resistances but helping candidates become friendly with them has become clear to me after many years of teaching psychoanalytic theory and tech- nique, supervising candidates, and doing psychoanalytic work. Anna Freud^ said, "When he (the analyst), sets about the work of enlightenment, he takes his stand at a point equidistant from the id, the ego and the superego" (p. 28). There are many resistances coming from various parts of the mind (psychic apparatus) that one must find on the way to uncovering the repressed. Even though we sit equidistant from different 34 Resistance: Friend or Foe? parts of the psychic apparatus, the id and superego must be understood as operating through the ego. A resistance, regardless of its source, is triggered by anxiety, conscious or unconscious. The relationships among conflict, resistance and anxiety are strong. Freud^ described the ego as (a) the seat of anxiety, (b) anxiety as a response of the ego and the role of the ego in producing anxiety, and (c) its role in defense and symptom formation. In the addenda of the same paper, he describes five types of resistances emanating from the three parts of the psychic apparatus: from the ego, (1) defense mechanisms, repression being the basis of all defense mechanisms, (2) the transference resistance and (3) gain from illness; from the id (4) repetition compulsion; from \h& superego (5) the need for punishment. RESISTANCES OF THE EGO DEFENSE MECHANISMS Freud used the theoretical model of repression as a prototype of other defensive procedures. In a strict sense, repression is an operation where an individual attempts to repel or to confine to the unconscious mental representations, thoughts, images, memories, and feelings that have been bound to a drive. When a drive derivative is pressing for satisfaction that may give the individual pleasure, and when satisfaction of that drive derivative might provoke unpleasure due to other reasons, i.e., environmental de- mands, it is repressed. To put it another way, the first of the five resistances include repression, and other defense methods used by the ego to ward off unconscious material that would arouse anxiety. In working with the defense mechanisms of patients, who are not conscious of them at the beginning of analysis, we must learn thoroughly all the different types of defensive maneuvers, i.e., displacement, projection, reaction formation, and so on. At the same time, we must understand how each individual uses clusters of defense mechanisms and compromise formations in the way they relate to the analyst, to themselves and to the world. Learning the whole list of defense mechanisms is a simple task in itself. One only has to read thoroughly Anna Freud's The Ego and the Mechanism of Defense^ or Ralph Greenson's The Technique and Practice of Psychoanalysis!^ Greenson lists the resistances according to source, fixation points, type of defense, and diagnostic categories. However, the real under- standing comes from learning how, when, and why a particular patient uses a particular defense in the course of analysis. Often a supervisee is quick to point out a defense intellectually and is eager to point it out immediately to patients without understanding what is prompting the defense. Why is a given patient using it at this time? To point 35 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY out defenses to patients does not, in reality, help them and, in all likelihood, will make them feel criticized, thereby impeding the work. What is helpful is to explore with the supervisee where patients go in their associations after having exhibited a defense mechanism. Where the associations go gives the analyst information about what is prompting the use of a particular defense. By exploring the associations to the defense, patients themselves will get back to what they were defending against, A defense acknowledged by a patient to the analyst helps make that patient a partner in the exploratory process, Freud ^° says, "The doctor has nothing else to do than to wait and let things take their course, a course that cannot be avoided nor always hastened. If he holds fast to this conviction, he will often be spared the illusion of having failed when, in fact, he is conducting the treatment on the right lines" (p, 55), Vignette 1 Ms, A, avoided (a defense mechanism), or rationalized whenever the topic of money arose in analysis, I did not ask her, "What prompts you to avoid?" I asked her, "What comes to mind?" Her associations then led to what it was that led her to want to get high on drugs and this, eventually, led to associations about how she and her father got high on drugs when she was fifteen years old. By not "addressing" her defensive avoidance of money, her free associations led to using drugs and her incestuous relationship with father around drugs. These matters became focal points of the analysis without ever bringing up the matter of money. As deeper material unfolded, Ms, A,, herself, said, "I always avoid talking about money because it reminds me of how broke I get and how anxious about drugs I get. It reminds me of my father and it gets me very upset when I talk about him," TRANSFERENCE RESISTANCE The aim of the transference resistance is to avoid memory work by keeping alive specific relationships whose prototypes stem from the infantile sexual developmental years. These infantile prototypes re-emerge in the transference with the analyst and are experienced with a strong sensation of immediacy. The analyst asks patients to remember but what they do, in fact, is to repeat. The transference and the reenactment to the analyst as a transference object, especially in the beginning part of treatment, is an ally. Classically, the transference is acknowledged to "be the terrain on which all the basic problems of a given analysis play themselves out; the establish- ment, modalities, interpretation and resolution of the transference are, in fact, what define the cure"" (p, 455), Freud* stated, "The transference resistance, , ,since it succeeds in establishing a relation to the analytic 36 Resistance: Friend or Foe? situation or the analyst himself and thus re-animating a repression which should only have been recollected" (p, 160), Here again, we use the idea of free association as one of our best allies in helping patients give up resistances. Patients may be relating to us in a manner showing a distortion of the reality of who we really are. By being defensive and telling the patient, "I am not that person," patients will feel more anxiety ridden and no good has been done. Just clarifying a distortion in the transference by negating the transference manifestation of patients is simply an intellectual exercise, not an emotional one. By being open about the transference manifestation and exploring with patients what prompts them to see us thus, the associations may, in time, lead to the infantile genetic roots of the distortion. There are many times when, patients will have a transference manifestation that, when we examine it closely, we may find it not to be such a distortion. What patients feel toward the analyst may have some reality in it. The important thing is to clarify with patients but neither agree nor negate the observation. By clarifying and exploring what prompts the feeling, what comes to mind, patients will, through free association, provide the material to be analyzed. Vignette 2 Mr, C, had been in treatment with me for a number of years, showing no apparent like nor dislike of me. He never got angry. He came on time, paid his fee on time, talked about his life in a monotone with little affect, and rarely brought me into his associations. After I told him I was going on vacation (the third year of analysis), he began to devalue me, criticize my office, denigrate the office furnishings for the first time. The patient had shown no reactions to previous vacations, I was aware of the shift and the fact that he had begun to show feelings toward me with affect. In time, I asked, "Do you have any thoughts about my vacation?" He answered that he had no thoughts about me at all or about my vacation while he continued his criticisms in a general way. Later, I asked him, "Are you aware of how you are talking to me?" His response was that he was unaware of any difference and continued his criticizing but with even more affect, "What is your need to devalue me and my office?" He replied, "I talk to everyone in the same way I talk to you," His transference was becoming more explicit and he was beginning to repeat with me as he did with others , The vacation might have been the trigger but, if I had pushed this interpretation without the associations of the patient, I would have missed the deeper material. It sometimes takes a long time before the transference becomes explicit. In psychoanalysis, one must never assume. Had I assumed that his change in 37 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY behavior was the.result of denial about being upset that I was going on vacation, I could not have explored with him his repetitions in the transfer- ence with me, repetitions he indicated he uses with his wife, his friends, and other people important to him. The patient is a participant in the analytic process. Fine'^ writes, "The first and most important lesson for the therapist to learn is to pay very careful attention to what the patient says and how he or she behaves. Through this minute examination of the patient's behavior, the therapist makes inferences about the transference reactions that the patient is experiencing. It is only to be expected that the situation at the beginning of therapy, with its numerous transferences and resistances, leaves even the experienced therapist bewil- dered. To be baffled by the patient is the mark of a good psychotherapist. It takes time to get to know another person; one can do so only by finding out a great deal about his or her life" (p. 30). Transference is a universal phenomenon and, in psychoanalysis, an intense one. It sometimes begins before the first phone call and it is very powerful. The analyst does not seek out transference; it is a product of the neurotic conflict of the patient. Even though it is considered a resistance, it is a phenomenon of which the analyst must be sensitive and respectful whether it be based on present day reality or not. It can be explicit or implied. The analyst must be receptive, totally open and non-defensive, with all transfer- ence manifestations of patients, even when manifestations are based on something realistic. "We all have deep inside feelings of sexuality, aggression, desperation, terror, anxiety, guilt, frustration, and, at times, a sense of helplessness and hopelessness. Patients are often unaware of these deep-seated feelings and cover them with hostility, manipulation behavior, acting out, binges, panic, tremendous denial, and avoidance of what brought them into treatment in the first place. If we tend to disregard our anxiety as a signal and clue to the feelings being evoked in us, either by the patient or by oiar own genetic history, we could become fiooded by the patient's desperation, seduced by the patient, frightened by the patient's hostility, and angered by the manipulations and acting out behaviors, which in turn can develop a sense of hopelessness in ourselves"'Mp. H). GAIN FROM ILLNESS Gain from illness covers all direct or indirect satisfactions that patients draw from their condition. Patients draw satisfaction from the symptom. It is like a flight into illness and, at times, patients perceive it resulting in 38 Resistance: Friend or Foe? beneficial change. Its appearance is in the shape of an extra advantage derived from an already established illness. The satisfactions involved are narcissistic or associated with self-preservation rather than directly libidinal. Gain from illness is a difficult resistance for the analyst to get friendly with because patients can get so much gratification from certain types of behavior that they don't want to give it up. It takes a great amount of patience on the part of the analyst to become friendly with the resistance of these patients before the analyst can start helping them recognize that the gratification or satisfaction from this resistance is not as gratifying as it seems. When the analyst is extremely patient with this resistance, he can, in a very slow and empathic manner, help patients see that this repeated behavior, which may give some momentary satisfaction, defeats the ability to grow. Vignette 3 Mr. B. had entered treatment with numerous difficulties in life. Unem- ployed and living alone, he was isolated and enraged with most of the world. Over the first five years of treatment, there was a great deal of silence in sessions. It became extremely taxing for me. Silence is a perplexing resis- tance. At various times in sessions, I asked quietly, "What is the silence about?" or "What comes to mind?" or "What are you feeling?" or "What are you thinking?" Usually the response was silence, sometimes accompa- nied by a smirk on his face. To go after the resistance too soon would only increase the resistance. There were times when I had to work hard to come to terms with my own impatience and with the recalcitrance of the patient. I had to keep trying to understand the man's need for silence. I saw it as thwarting any satisfaction on my part to get work done. Yet I learned from this patient early in my career the importance of sitting with a very silent patient and being comfortable with the way he related. It became clear to me that this tvas the work, sitting comfortably with the silence, and that the silence itself was the way this patient related. Being able to get friendly with this man's resistance was a signpost to me and it opened up the entire analysis. My initial feeling of defeat and being ignored helped me understand and empathize with the plight of the patient. Only then, could I understand and accept that it was the patient who was leading the analysis and not me. Excessive silence is often a sign of despair. In time, the associations of this patient verified his despair. As I became less anxious with the resistances of this patient, the patient himself became less resistant to his own dynamics and the analysis became more of an emotional experience. It was the emotional aspect and not the intellectual that made the difference. 39 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY It is noteworthy that over the years this patient continued to come, week in and week out, although much of the early work accomplished was on a nonverbal level. I can only imagine, although in analysis nothing can be assumed, that he was able to come in because he could be silent and feel whatever he felt without telling me what it was. Later in the analysis, when the patient became more verbal, he told me my silence and the absence of pushing him to produce material developed a feeling of safety with himself and with me. There came a time when I was aware that this man had difficulty becoming friendly with me. I turned this thought into an interpretation and said to him one day, "Are you aware that you have difficulty becoming friendly with me?" Very slowly, over time, the patient began to reveal his extremely sadistic fantasies of killing himself and killing others although each revelation was, again, followed by long periods of silence. From that point on, the analysis began to change and he slowly began to speak about his childhood, his rage at the world and how being silent was a way to get people to feel sorry for him. Until that point, silence was the only way he knew how to express his rage, a way that made other people uncomfortable. In the course of his analysis, he was able to verbalize his feelings, form a love relationship and find meaningful employment. ID RESISTANCE The id resistance, repetition compulsion, in itself, causes pain. It is an unconscious need to repeat certain behaviors that may stand in the way of change and, at times, deliberately places patients in distressing situations by repeating old experiences they do not recall. This resistance, arising from the id, necessitates the "working through process" in analysis. Freud^" discusses the concept of the repetition compulsion. He states, "The first step in overcoming the resistance is made, as we know, by the analyst uncovering the resistance, which is never recognized by the patient and acquainting him with it" (p. 155). "Beginners in analytic practice are inclined to look on this introductory step as constituting the whole of their work. The analyst had merely forgotten that giving the resistance a name could not result in its immediate cessation. One must allow the patient time to become more conversant with this resistance with which he has now become acquainted, to work through it, to overcome it, by continuing in defiance of it the analytic work according to the fundamental rule of analysis" (p. 155). In teaching and in supervising, candidates/supervisees tend to use the repetition compulsion in much the same way as patients do. It is important for the teacher/supervisor to recognize in the candidates/supervisees, just as 40 Resistance: Friend or Foe? it is important to recognize in patients, the use of repetition compulsion and to explore and use it as a teaching tool. Candidates and supervisees as much as patients must learn to be comfortable with their id resistances to new material. It is one way of teaching them to be comfortable with id resistances of their patients. Candidates and supervisees as well as patients develop resistances, resistances to learning new and difficult, often anxiety-producing, material. I have found it effective to turn the repetition compulsion around by repeating the same material again and again in as many ways as I can, as creatively as I can with candidates, with supervisees and with patients. Without judging either them or myself for doing so, by making a positive use of it, I can help them learn to become more accepting of this particular resistance, repetition, and not feel intimidated by it. "How do you feel," I ask my candidates/ supervisees,"about my repetition of the material?" Their response is always positive at which point I emphasize, "Keep in mind that your patients will need the same creative repetitions and you must learn to be comfortable with that fact." SUPEREGO RESISTANCE This resistance coming from the superego seems to originate from a sense of guilt and need for punishment; and, at times, opposes every move toward success and can oppose success in the analysis (negative therapeutic reac- tion). Guilt and self-punishing tendencies are the result of conflict between the superego and the ego. The superego is the heir of the Oedipus complex and is constituted through the internalization of parental prohibitions and demands. This resistance is a formidable one. I say that because, first of all, analysts themselves must have had a long and deep personal analysis to reduce their own harsh superego. Secondly, the analyst must become friendly with the, often extreme, guilt feelings of patients. The fantasy life of patients, often held in check by guilt, is the primary material of the analysis. Conversely, individuals who have guilt feelings are motivated to be in treatment. The ideal is a balance between conscious fantasy life and guilt feelings but, when patients enter analysis, one, both or neither may be conscious. The beginning work in the analysis is to help patients become conscious of their fantasy life and their sense of guilt. Here the idea of getting friendly with the patients' feelings of guilt is of the utmost importance since, if the analyst does not, the guilt of patients can cause the analyst to feel sorry for them, rush to try to absolve them of guilt, use a reality interpretation or give forms of supportive, reassuring remarks, 41 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY none of which are effective in treatment. Patients can get lost in the guilt, unaware of the conflict causing the guilt. If we help patients become more tolerant of their anxiety and gioilt feelings, it is possible, then, to begin separating the guilt feelings from the conflict causing it. In this manner, the analysis is enriched. A long period of time must be spent on superego analysis in the beginning years of treatment. Even once the harsh superego begins to diminish and a new more benign introject starts to become intemalized, the analyst must be aware of the reassertion of the harsh superego infantile introject. In supervising candidates, I find that supervisees tend to put themselves into what I call a "masochistic orgy" whenever they feel they have erred, missed material, overlooked a resistance, or when patients leave treatment abruptly. It is useful to help supervisees explore, not only the cause of the supervisee's guilt, but the reason for its intensity, and to share the idea that some guilt can be helpful in examining one's work. It leads to thoroughness and discipline essential for an analyst. Candidates must be aware of their own superego, the intensity of their own guilt and the reason for it, all material they need to take into their own personal analysis. In time, the analytic superego becomes more benign after which the guilt and anxiety of the analyst can be used as a signal, a signpost, leading to a piece of material in need of deeper scrutiny. As self-criticism changes to a critical self-awareness, the empathy required to effectively practice psychoanalysis is freed. One of the reasons guilt feelings can be so painful is that they can lead an individual to experience a feeling of annihilation and a cessation of narcissis- tic supplies. Feelings of guilt result when patients perceive their wishes, desires, and needs as unacceptable and forbidden. It is the analyst's consistent working through and acceptance of those wishes that helps a new and benign introject to start to form. By consistently analyzing patients' transference manifestations, so often accompanied by guilt feelings, in an open and accepting manner, patients may, in time, also become more open to explore their need to hold onto the harshness of their own superego. In some sense, the ego begins to expand when patients are able to tolerate the anxiety and guilt feelings consciously and, at the same time, explore what has produced them. As patients become more aware of their own harsh superego mandates, inhibitions, and anxieties, their whole inner world opens up for them. Then they can begin to understand on a deeper level their own psychic structure, compromise formations and how, in many ways, they, themselves, have contributed to their own script in life. In turn, as the ego expands, they can begin to change those contributions and take charge of their own lives. 42 Resistance: Friend or Foe? One of the most important aspects of psychoanalysis is the reduction of a harsh superego. Like transference resistance, this resistance can reappear over time in the analysis. If we become friendly with the repetition of the reappearance of the harsh superego, and not short tempered to see it return once it seemed to have gone, the patient is helped not to be short tempered with it but rather to question, why it has reasserted itself. Fine^'' wrote, "I would argue that the proper use of countertransference leads to continual self-analysis on the part of the analyst of the most effective kind because it forces the subject (the analyst this time) to face the most painful and embarrassing transferences, even if he does not share this information with anyone. This self-analysis not only takes the sting out of difficulties experienced in the course of doing an analysis but allows the enhancement of the pleasure of being an analyst by the very same mecha- nism that helps the patient, namely the reduction of the severity of the superego" (p. 7). CONCLUSION As a result of my work in the beginning years of my practice I began to form in my mind the need for analysts to become friendly with resistances and the need to help patients become friendly with them as well. One of the major tenets of psychoanalysis is to help individuals expand the ego, in other words, the ego must become consciously aware of what it was not aware of at the beginning of analysis. By working in the manner presented in this short paper and viewing resistances benignly, patients develop the ability to tolerate consciously the discomfort that results in the search for an expanded ego. The realization that there is an unconscious, and that each of us has his/her own individual psychology, is among the most significant contribu- tions Freud made to us. By being disciplined in our work, by building on and being true to Freud's psychoanalytic method and the psychoanalytic situa- tion,'' by expanding on our Freudian base through knowledge that has evolved and continues to evolve in the first hundred years of the art and science of psychoanalysis, and by being consistent in our work with patients, psychoanalysts have the good fortune and the freedom to derive libidinal satisfaction through creatively striving toward the ultimate goal: helping patients discover for themselves their unconscious. It is then that our patients have the greatest opportunity to expand the ego and to attain love. As Freud explained, "The working through of the resistances may, in practice, turn out to be an arduous task for the subject of the analysis and a trial of patience for the analyst. Nevertheless, it is a part of the work that 43 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY effects the greatest change in patients and distinguishes anal)^ic treatment from any kind of treatment by suggestion. From a theoretical point of view, one may correlate it with the 'abreacting' of the quotas of affect strangulated by repression—an abreaction without which hypnotic treatment remained ineffective''^^ (pp. 155-56). SUMMARY It is not only individual patients who are resistant to analysis, it is our society itself. We Hve in a society that demands fast results. In the field of mental health, the emphasis is on the quick fix leading to many types of therapy that have evolved including short-term therapy and drug therapy. As psychoanalysts, we know that no real structural change can occur in a human being without working on the unconscious. Psychoanalysis must be the treatment of choice if lasting change is the goal. Resistance to psychoanalysis is largely the resistance to the very existence of the unconscious, to the idea that part of human motivation lies in the unknown but such is the case in groups, in society, as well as in individuals. It is the task of the psychoanalyst to maintain the psychoanalytic stance, to become friendly with the resistances and to be part of the healing process that must involve a deep understanding and acceptance of the unconscious, its motives and its resistances.
